title: Concentration times area does not determine an amount
revised_question: Reconstruction: Which volume or depth is missing from the calculation, what do exact unit conversions give, and can the requested amount be identified from concentration and area alone?
status: Developed mathematical repair with exact worked checks; historical evidence is assistant-only
summary: The recovered calculation contains a dimensional defect before any numerical approximation is considered. Concentration measures amount per volume, whereas the supplied spatial quantity is an area. Their product has amount per length, so an amount cannot be inferred without a depth or volume model. The molar conversion at the end can be correct while the preceding quantity is ill-defined. This entry develops only the mathematics of that error, not an environmental prescription.

For a nonuniform domain use a depth function h(x) and a concentration field C(x,z) in a common consistent unit system."]
theorem_name: An exact missing-depth law and nonidentifiability
theorem_statement: For a uniform slab with the stipulated inputs, m(h)=558.45h kg when h is measured in metres. Without h or an equivalent volume constraint, the amount is not identified. The source fragment’s 10^6L/km³ factor is also incorrect: the exact factor is 10^12L/km³.
theorem_proof: The volume is 10^7h m³=10^10h L. Multiplying by 10^(−6)mol/L gives 10^4h mol; multiplying by 55.845g/mol gives 558450h g=558.45h kg. At every step the units cancel to the required quantity. Holding C and A fixed while replacing h by sh for any s>0 leaves all supplied concentration and area data unchanged but multiplies the amount by s. Thus those data alone cannot distinguish different amounts. For a variable concentration or depth, integrate the local amount density over the actual volume. Constant C gives C∫_A h(x)dA, so even then the required extra datum is the area-integrated depth. Bounds C_min≤C≤C_max and h_min≤h≤h_max yield corresponding integral bounds, but an area by itself supplies neither.

title: Stored energy needs a state function and a power balance
revised_question: Reconstruction: What extra state relation is needed to turn charge into an energy quantity, and how does a specified lumped model account for delivered power and loss?
status: Developed mathematical repair with exact worked checks; historical evidence is assistant-only
summary: This entry is a new mathematical reconstruction of a recovered qualitative concept. The source does not contain the equations below. The useful correction is to distinguish charge, voltage, energy and power instead of treating a carrier count or a metaphor as an energy calculation. A simple declared state model is enough to show what information a quantitative answer would require.
definitions_json: ["Charge q is measured in coulombs, current I in coulombs per second, voltage in joules per coulomb, energy in joules and power in joules per second.","Let q∈[0,Q] denote remaining charge. Prescribe a continuous open-circuit voltage function V_oc(q) and define the model storage function E(q)=∫_0^q V_oc(s)ds.","For discharge take I(t)≥0, qdot=−I, resistance R≥0 and terminal voltage V(t)=V_oc(q(t))−RI(t). This is a stated lumped model, not a complete electrochemical description."]
theorem_name: An exact balance law for the prescribed storage model
theorem_statement: Along an absolutely continuous charge trajectory with integrable power terms, Edot=−V_oc(q)I almost everywhere. Therefore Edot+P_out+P_loss=0 with P_out=VI and P_loss=RI². Charge capacity Q alone does not determine stored energy: the voltage-state law is also required.
theorem_proof: The fundamental theorem of calculus gives E′(q)=V_oc(q). Applying the chain rule to qdot=−I yields Edot=−V_oc(q)I. The terminal relation gives P_out=(V_oc−RI)I, and adding RI² recovers V_ocI, proving the identity. Integration from t0 to t1 gives E(q(t0))−E(q(t1))=∫P_out dt+∫RI²dt. The loss is nonnegative because R≥0. To prove nonidentifiability from charge alone, compare two constant laws V_oc(q)=v1 and V_oc(q)=v2 with v1≠v2: both allow the same Q but give E(Q)=v1Q and v2Q. For a variable law the correct quantity is its integral, not an arbitrarily selected endpoint voltage times Q.

Because one watt-hour is 3600J, these values are 3.5Wh, 0.2Wh and 3.3Wh. Terminal voltage decreases from 3.8V to 2.8V and remains positive in this example. These parameters were selected for the worked mathematics and were not recovered from the 2024 passage.","conclusion":"The model turns an imprecise storage metaphor into a transparent differential and integral calculation, while preserving the distinction between source evidence and newly supplied mathematics."}

The model omits temperature, hysteresis, state-dependent losses and other effects, and its identity holds for its declared assumptions rather than for every real device.

title: Picard classes and the Néron–Severi quotient
revised_question: Which equivalence relation on line bundles is intended, and which part is discrete enough to have a finite rank?
status: Classical result or corrected formulation with a worked example
summary: On P¹×P¹, NS(X)=Pic(X)≅Z² with fiber-class intersection matrix [[0,1],[1,0]]. The class (a,b) has self-intersection 2ab. For a,b≥0, its space of sections has dimension (a+1)(b+1). The finite-rank divisor quotient is a well-defined geometric object. It is different from an unspecified real vector space obtained by tensoring every line bundle with R.
definitions_json: ["For a smooth projective complex variety, Pic(X) is the abelian group of line bundles under tensor product. Pic⁰(X) denotes the subgroup algebraically equivalent to zero.","The Néron–Severi theorem makes NS(X) a finitely generated abelian group. Its real vector space has finite dimension ρ(X). This background theorem is not proved by a two-dimensional matrix check.","On X=P¹×P¹, write O(a,b) for the external tensor product of the two degree-a and degree-b bundles."]
theorem_name: Picard classes and the Néron–Severi quotient
theorem_statement: On P¹×P¹, NS(X)=Pic(X)≅Z² with fiber-class intersection matrix [[0,1],[1,0]]. The class (a,b) has self-intersection 2ab. For a,b≥0, its space of sections has dimension (a+1)(b+1).
theorem_proof: The projective-bundle description of the product gives the two independent fiber classes and no Pic⁰ component. Two fibers of the same projection are disjoint and equivalent, so each fiber class squares to zero. A fiber of one projection meets a fiber of the other in one point; bilinearity gives (aF₁+bF₂)²=2ab. Sections of O(a,b) are bihomogeneous polynomials of bidegree (a,b). Their monomial basis consists of the (a+1) choices of first-factor exponent and (b+1) choices of second-factor exponent, proving the dimension formula directly. These explicit calculations use the product structure; they do not imply that Picard groups of arbitrary varieties are free of rank two.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Take O(2,3) on the product and compare it with O(1,0).","calculation":"The first class has twelve independent sections and self-intersection twelve. The second has two sections and self-intersection zero. Both are discrete divisor classes, whereas on an elliptic curve the degree-zero line bundles form a positive-dimensional Picard variety and cannot be replaced by a single rank count.","conclusion":"The finite-rank divisor quotient is a well-defined geometric object. It is different from an unspecified real vector space obtained by tensoring every line bundle with R."}
limits: Picard number does not classify a variety or its automorphism group. Torsion in NS and continuous Pic⁰ information can be lost after tensoring with R. Statements about singular or nonprojective spaces require different hypotheses.

title: Replace Picard intransigence by a defined fixed-space calculation
revised_question: What finite-dimensional representation is being acted on, and which rank or invariant subspace is actually measured?
status: Classical result or corrected formulation with a worked example
summary: For a finite real representation, P=|G|⁻¹Σ_gρ(g) is a projection onto V^G. Its kernel is the span of all ρ(g)v−v. For the factor-swap involution of P¹×P¹, the invariant divisor subspace has dimension one. A repaired invariant is now computable and its blindness is exhibited, rather than hidden behind a new name.
definitions_json: ["A representation of a finite group G on V assigns linear maps ρ(g) compatible with composition. Its fixed space is V^G={v:ρ(g)v=v for every g}.","For pullback actions, one may use g↦(g⁻¹)* to obtain a left representation; for an involution this convention makes no difference.","The retrieved label “Picard intransigence” is nonstandard and does not by itself define a linear map whose corank could be taken."]
theorem_name: Replace Picard intransigence by a defined fixed-space calculation
theorem_statement: For a finite real representation, P=|G|⁻¹Σ_gρ(g) is a projection onto V^G. Its kernel is the span of all ρ(g)v−v. For the factor-swap involution of P¹×P¹, the invariant divisor subspace has dimension one.
theorem_proof: Multiplying P by ρ(h) merely permutes the summands, so every vector Pv is fixed. Conversely a fixed vector is unchanged by averaging, hence P acts as its identity and P²=P. Each difference ρ(g)v−v is killed by P. In the other direction v−Pv is an average of v−ρ(g)v, so every kernel vector belongs to the difference span. This proves the decomposition without assigning a vague scalar to the group itself. In the product-surface basis F₁,F₂, the swap is J=[[0,1],[1,0]], and P=(I+J)/2. Its image is span(F₁+F₂), while its kernel is span(F₁−F₂).
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Use the factor swap and an automorphism acting by a nontrivial Möbius transformation on the first P¹ factor only.","calculation":"The swap has rank(J−I)=1 and fixed dimension one. The factorwise Möbius automorphism acts trivially on both divisor classes, so its induced matrix is I despite being a nonidentity geometric map. Thus zero action rank does not mean the geometric automorphism is trivial.","conclusion":"A repaired invariant is now computable and its blindness is exhibited, rather than hidden behind a new name."}
limits: Averaging over an infinite group is not justified by a finite sum. Finite generation and the choice of coefficient field matter. This calculation does not supply a complete invariant of Picard varieties or automorphism groups.
extension: For finitely many specified automorphisms, stack the matrices g*−I and calculate their common kernel. Compare this exact fixed lattice with the coarser real subspace and identify the geometric information that both fail to detect.

title: Independent variations give separate Euler–Lagrange equations
revised_question: Which functional, admissible variations and boundary conditions make the proposed variational equation meaningful?
status: Classical result or corrected formulation with a worked example
summary: Stationarity under every pair (ξ,η) is equivalent to the two residual equations. Stationarity only along η=κξ generally imposes just E_x+κE_y=0 and can miss genuine directions. The revised model separates a variational derivation, a constraint on variations and a degeneracy of the functional.
definitions_json: ["Let x,y be smooth paths on [0,T] with fixed endpoints, and let ξ,η be independent smooth variations vanishing there.","The Euler–Lagrange residuals are E_x=L_x−d(L_ẋ)/dt and E_y=L_y−d(L_ẏ)/dt.","A weighting symbol must have a defined domain and value. It cannot replace the independent test functions required by a variational principle."]
theorem_name: Independent variations give separate Euler–Lagrange equations
theorem_statement: Stationarity under every pair (ξ,η) is equivalent to the two residual equations. Stationarity only along η=κξ generally imposes just E_x+κE_y=0 and can miss genuine directions.
theorem_proof: Differentiate S[x+εξ,y+εη] at ε=0 and integrate the velocity terms by parts. Endpoint terms vanish, leaving δS=∫(E_xξ+E_yη)dt. First choose η=0 and arbitrary ξ, then ξ=0 and arbitrary η. The fundamental lemma gives each residual zero. If variations are restricted to η=κξ, the same reasoning gives only their weighted sum. This is a different constrained problem. In finite dimensions, S(a,b)=a−b has gradient (1,−1). Its derivative along the diagonal direction (1,1) vanishes everywhere, although it has no unconstrained stationary point. This simple counterexample disproves the idea that one cancelling sum certifies all variations.

At κ=0, the functional sees no y variation and every admissible y has the same contribution. The rank loss is an exact parameter stratum, not evidence that an undefined geometric coefficient creates an extra field law.","conclusion":"The revised model separates a variational derivation, a constraint on variations and a degeneracy of the functional."}
limits: The calculation assumes sufficient regularity for differentiation and integration by parts. Weak solutions require a specified function space. Stationarity is not automatically minimality; the second variation must be checked.
extension: For the oscillator action ∫(q̇²−ω²q²)/2, test q=εsin(πt/T). Its action is ε²T[(π/T)²−ω²]/4, negative when T>π/ω. This explicitly shows why the phrase least action must be handled as stationary action. For T<π/ω, the Poincaré inequality ∫q̇²≥(π/T)²∫q² proves positivity of the quadratic action for all zero-endpoint paths. The same time threshold therefore marks a real change in the second variation.

theorem_statement: The normalized derivative is p_t=(1/3−x²)/(t+1/3)², whose integral is zero. At t=1, S=(7/6)−π/4−log(3/2), and Ṡ=(10−3π)/16>0.

title: A complexity score requires units, weights and a stated inference
revised_question: What can a specified scalar aggregate of features distinguish, and which conclusions require more than naming the aggregate?
status: Classical result or corrected formulation with a worked example

title: Hamilton, Hamilton–Jacobi and Riccati equations meet at a caustic
revised_question: Reconstruction: How are Hamilton’s equations related to the Hamilton–Jacobi PDE, how does a quadratic phase produce a Riccati equation, and why can that Riccati variable blow up while the mechanical trajectory remains smooth?
status: Classical mathematics newly developed from a recovered assistant-only catalog name
summary: Three separately named catalog items can be made concrete with one harmonic oscillator. title: A cubic Routh–Hurwitz test with an exact stability boundary
revised_question: Reconstruction: For a real monic cubic, which coefficient inequalities are equivalent to strict left-half-plane stability, and where does s³+2s²+2s+K lose that property?
status: Classical mathematics newly developed from a recovered assistant-only catalog name
summary: The stability criterion is most useful when it gives a parameter certificate rather than a list of approximate roots. A cubic is small enough that the criterion can be proved directly from its possible real and complex factors. The equality boundary also reveals why strict inequalities are required.
definitions_json: ["A real polynomial is strictly Hurwitz when every complex root has negative real part. This is the spectral condition relevant to an autonomous linear ODE with that characteristic polynomial.","Write p(s)=s³+as²+bs+c with real a,b,c. Strict cubic Hurwitz conditions are a>0, b>0, c>0 and ab>c.","When a≠0, the cubic Routh first column is 1,a,(ab−c)/a,c. theorem_name: Necessary and sufficient cubic inequalities
theorem_statement: The monic real cubic is strictly Hurwitz if and only if a,b,c>0 and ab>c. In the family p_K=s³+2s²+2s+K, this holds exactly for 0<K<4. At K=4 the factorization is (s+2)(s²+2), so the imaginary pair prevents strict stability.
theorem_proof: If all three roots are negative real numbers, write their negatives r₁,r₂,r₃>0. The elementary symmetric coefficient formulas make a,b,c positive, and expanding ab−c gives a sum of positive terms. If an unstable nonreal pair u±iv with u≥0 existed, the remaining real root would be −r with r>0, since c=r(u²+v²)>0. Factoring p=(s+r)(s²−2us+u²+v²) then gives ab−c=−2u[(r−u)²+v²]≤0, contradicting ab>c. All roots therefore lie strictly left of the imaginary axis. Applying the inequalities to a=b=2 gives K>0 and 4>K, as claimed.

At the surface ∂_ru_r=0, so after subtracting the irrelevant constant pressure, σ_rr=(3μU/(2a))cosθ. The shear component is σ_rθ=μ(∂_ru_θ−u_θ/r+r^(−1)∂_θu_r)=−(3μU/(2a))sinθ there. The z component of traction is σ_rrcosθ−σ_rθsinθ=3μU/(2a), independent of θ. Integrating over area 4πa² gives 6πμaU. Equivalently the pressure contributes 2πμaU and shear contributes 4πμaU. Switching from incoming fluid velocity to body velocity reverses the sign. For settling, equate the magnitude 6πμaV_t to the net weight (4π/3)a³Δρg and cancel common factors to obtain the terminal formula. Thus the coefficient is derived from the explicit stress field, while the governing exterior solution itself is a stated classical input.

title: Specify the clustering objective before adding weights
revised_question: Which definitions of between-cluster separation and within-cluster scatter actually create independent objectives?
status: Corrected formulation or classical result with an explicit worked example
summary: T=W+B. For nonnegative a,b with a+b>0, maximizing aB−bW over the same partitions gives exactly the minimizers of W. An added spatial or graph term can create a new tradeoff, but two copies of the same scatter information do not. The revised objective states what each term contributes and which weights are identifiable from the minimizers.
definitions_json: ["A partition consists of nonempty clusters C_j, sizes n_j and centroids μ_j. The global centroid is μ.","Define W=Σ_jΣ_{i∈C_j}||x_i−μ_j||², B=Σ_jn_j||μ_j−μ||² and T=Σ_i||x_i−μ||².","These definitions apply to a fixed dataset and fixed Euclidean metric. An objective also needs a direction of optimization, admissible partitions and explicit weights."]
theorem_name: Specify the clustering objective before adding weights
theorem_statement: T=W+B. For nonnegative a,b with a+b>0, maximizing aB−bW over the same partitions gives exactly the minimizers of W. An added spatial or graph term can create a new tradeoff, but two copies of the same scatter information do not.
theorem_proof: Write x_i−μ=(x_i−μ_j)+(μ_j−μ) for i in cluster j. Expand its squared norm. The cross term sums to zero because Σ_{i∈C_j}(x_i−μ_j)=0. Summing proves the decomposition. Substituting B=T−W into aB−bW gives aT−(a+b)W. The first term is independent of the partition, which proves the optimizer statement, including all ties. This derivation prevents an apparently richer objective from concealing a redundant parameter. If cluster count is unrestricted, singleton clusters give W=0; a complexity penalty or fixed count is then necessary to obtain a meaningful grouping problem.

Repeating the data coordinates with a changed scale changes T,W,B quadratically, so unrelated penalties must be scaled or normalized deliberately.","conclusion":"The revised objective states what each term contributes and which weights are identifiable from the minimizers."}

extension: For any proposed extra term R, exhibit two partitions with the same W but different R. Such a pair proves that R supplies information not already contained in Euclidean scatter. Otherwise simplify the objective before tuning its parameters.

title: Spatial coherence gives an exact cut-versus-fit threshold
revised_question: When does a spatial penalty improve a clustering model, and when does it erase a real boundary?
status: Corrected formulation or classical result with an explicit worked example
summary: For γ≥0, the optimum is min(γ,1). The true split 00|11 is uniquely optimal as an unlabeled partition for γ<1; the one-cluster partition is uniquely optimal for γ>1; both tie at γ=1. Spatial regularization is a tunable mathematical preference with a measurable failure mode. It is not an automatic improvement independent of units or data contrast.

Use first label zero to enumerate eight cases exactly."]
theorem_name: Spatial coherence gives an exact cut-versus-fit threshold
theorem_statement: For γ≥0, the optimum is min(γ,1). The true split 00|11 is uniquely optimal as an unlabeled partition for γ<1; the one-cluster partition is uniquely optimal for γ>1; both tie at γ=1.
theorem_proof: The all-equal partition has cut zero and W=1. Every nonconstant labeling on a connected path has at least one cut and W≥0, so its objective is at least γ. The labeling (0,0,1,1) has one cut and W=0, attaining that lower bound. For γ<1 it beats the constant partition. Equality in the nonconstant lower bound requires W=0, so no cluster can mix a zero and a one. With at most two clusters this forces exactly the split by value. For γ>1, every nonconstant partition has objective at least γ>1. The same argument gives only the two stated optima at equality; exhaustive enumeration independently checks the finite certificate.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Compare γ=1/2, γ=1 and γ=2 without refitting or rescaling the data.","calculation":"The split objectives are 1/2,1,2; the constant objective is always one. Thus increasing the spatial penalty crosses an exact boundary and eventually merges the two groups. Multiplying every observation by c multiplies W by c² but leaves cut unchanged, moving the threshold to γ=c².","conclusion":"Spatial regularization is a tunable mathematical preference with a measurable failure mode. limits: The proof uses this path, these observations and at most two clusters. More labels, normalized cuts, weighted edges or higher-dimensional data create different thresholds. A continuum perimeter limit needs additional scaling assumptions.
extension: On a larger finite graph, retain each partition’s pair (cut,W). Lower supporting lines of these points determine all parameter transitions. Dominated pairs can be discarded, yielding a compact exact certificate of the regularization path.

title: Three regularizers produce three different shrinkage rules
revised_question: Does the model penalize an ℓ₁ norm, an ℓ₂ norm or a squared ℓ₂ norm, and what solution does that choice actually imply?
status: Corrected formulation or classical result with an explicit worked example
summary: The solutions are componentwise soft threshold x_i=sign(z_i)max(|z_i|−λ,0), radial shrink x=max(1−λ/||z||₂,0)z, and ridge x=z/(1+λ), respectively. Writing ||M||₂ without stating whether M is a vector or a matrix is incomplete: a matrix spectral norm, Frobenius norm and entrywise norm lead to different optimization problems.
definitions_json: ["Fix z∈Rⁿ and λ>0. Strict convexity of the quadratic term gives a unique minimizer for each convex penalty.","The ℓ₁ penalty is λΣ|x_i|. The unsquared ℓ₂ penalty is λ√Σx_i². Ridge uses λ||x||₂²/2.","A subgradient g of a convex function f at x satisfies f(y)≥f(x)+gᵀ(y−x) for every y."]
theorem_name: Three regularizers produce three different shrinkage rules
theorem_statement: The solutions are componentwise soft threshold x_i=sign(z_i)max(|z_i|−λ,0), radial shrink x=max(1−λ/||z||₂,0)z, and ridge x=z/(1+λ), respectively.
theorem_proof: For ℓ₁ the coordinates separate. At a positive coordinate, optimality gives x_i−z_i+λ=0; at a negative one it gives x_i−z_i−λ=0. At zero, the subgradient interval [−λ,λ] contains z_i exactly when |z_i|≤λ. For the unsquared ℓ₂ norm and a nonzero solution, x−z+λx/||x||=0, so x points along z and its length is ||z||−λ. At zero, optimality requires z in the radius-λ Euclidean ball, giving the threshold case. Ridge is differentiable everywhere: x−z+λx=0. These conditions are sufficient by convexity and unique by strict convexity of the full objective.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Use z=(3,4), λ=1, and then a small first coordinate z=(1/2,4).","calculation":"For (3,4), soft threshold gives (2,3); radial shrink gives (12/5,16/5), since ||z||=5; ridge gives (3/2,2). For (1/2,4), ℓ₁ sets the first coordinate exactly to zero, while both other rules retain a nonzero first coordinate. Thus sparsity of individual coefficients follows from a specific corner geometry rather than from the generic word regularization.","conclusion":"Writing ||M||₂ without stating whether M is a vector or a matrix is incomplete: a matrix spectral norm, Frobenius norm and entrywise norm lead to different optimization problems."}
limits: The derivation concerns an identity quadratic data term. Replacing it with ||Ax−z||² generally destroys the coordinatewise closed form. It does not establish that any penalty identifies a scientifically correct model.
extension: For disjoint groups of coefficients, Σ_g||x_g||₂ yields one radial threshold per group. This keeps or removes entire groups and provides a precise intermediate choice between coordinate sparsity and uniform ridge shrinkage. Each of these proximal maps is nonexpansive: if outputs x,y correspond to inputs z,w, monotonicity of the convex subgradient gives〈(z−x)−(w−y),x−y〉≥0. Hence||x−y||²≤〈z−w,x−y〉≤||z−w||||x−y||, proving the unit Lipschitz bound.

title: An online centroid is a mean only for the right step sizes
revised_question: When is C_new=C_old+η(x_new−C_old) the sample mean, and when is it an exponentially weighted filter?
status: Corrected formulation or classical result with an explicit worked example
summary: With η_n=1/n and c₁=x₁, c_n=(x₁+⋯+x_n)/n. With constant η, c_n=rⁿc₀+ηΣ_{j=1}ⁿr^{n−j}x_j, E c_n=μ+rⁿ(c₀−μ), and Var(c_n)=ησ²(1−r^{2n})/(2−η). The update now has an explicit statistical interpretation and a calculable adaptation-versus-noise tradeoff.

Assignment of new points to a cluster is a separate problem from this update.","For the variance statement assume scalar independent x_n with common mean μ and variance σ², and a deterministic initial c₀.","For constant η define r=1−η. A forgetting factor r near one remembers more observations but adapts more slowly."]
theorem_name: An online centroid is a mean only for the right step sizes
theorem_statement: With η_n=1/n and c₁=x₁, c_n=(x₁+⋯+x_n)/n. With constant η, c_n=rⁿc₀+ηΣ_{j=1}ⁿr^{n−j}x_j, E c_n=μ+rⁿ(c₀−μ), and Var(c_n)=ησ²(1−r^{2n})/(2−η).
theorem_proof: The mean formula follows by induction after multiplying the recurrence by n. For constant η, repeated substitution gives the geometric expansion. Taking expectations and using ηΣ_{k=0}^{n−1}r^k=1−rⁿ yields the bias formula. Independence eliminates covariance cross terms, so variance is η²σ²Σ_{k=0}^{n−1}r^{2k}. Summing the geometric series and using 1−r²=η(2−η) gives the stated result. Its positive limit ησ²/(2−η) shows that fixed-step smoothing is not a consistent estimator of a static mean as n tends to infinity, although tracking a changing mean may motivate it.

Solve this forced recurrence to bound tracking lag from a stated drift bound rather than describing the algorithm as universally adaptive. Matching the stationary variance with the varianceσ²/n of an equally weighted mean gives an effective sample size n_eff=(2−η)/η. Atη=1/2 this is three, even after infinitely many observations. theorem_statement: For scalar x,y, k(x,y)=(1+xy)² is PSD, with φ(x)=(1,√2x,x²). By contrast k_bad(x,y)=1−xy fails PSD even on the two points −1 and one.

title: Bayesian uncertainty and data fusion depend on covariance
revised_question: How does an explicit probabilistic model combine observations, and why can duplicated evidence not count as independent precision?
status: Corrected formulation or classical result with an explicit worked example
summary: The posterior variance and mean are v=(v₀⁻¹+nσ⁻²)⁻¹ and m=v(m₀/v₀+Σy_i/σ²). If Y consists of n identical copies of a single noisy measurement, Σ=σ²11ᵀ and every unbiased weighted estimate has variance σ², not σ²/n. Fusion quality depends on dependence structure as much as on the number of input channels.
definitions_json: ["Let θ∼N(m₀,v₀) and y_i|θ be independent N(θ,σ²). Precision is reciprocal variance.","For a linear estimate wᵀY with E Y=θ1, unbiasedness is wᵀ1=1 and variance is wᵀΣw.","A posterior variance describes uncertainty under a stated model. It is not a model-free confidence guarantee."]
theorem_name: Bayesian uncertainty and data fusion depend on covariance
theorem_statement: The posterior variance and mean are v=(v₀⁻¹+nσ⁻²)⁻¹ and m=v(m₀/v₀+Σy_i/σ²). If Y consists of n identical copies of a single noisy measurement, Σ=σ²11ᵀ and every unbiased weighted estimate has variance σ², not σ²/n.
theorem_proof: The log posterior is, up to constants, −(θ−m₀)²/(2v₀)−Σ(y_i−θ)²/(2σ²). Collecting its quadratic and linear coefficients gives −(θ−m)²/(2v) plus a constant, which proves the update. A future independent observation adds σ² to the posterior predictive variance. For duplicated evidence, compute wᵀΣw=σ²(wᵀ1)²=σ². No choice of unbiased weights reduces it. Treating the n coordinates as independent replaces this singular covariance with σ²I and would manufacture precision absent from the observations.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Take m₀=0,v₀=1,σ²=1 and two independent observations y₁=1,y₂=2. Contrast them with two copies of the same observation.","calculation":"The independent-data posterior is N(1,1/3); a new observation has predictive variance 4/3. For two duplicated unit-variance measurements the average retains variance one, whereas two independent ones would average to variance one half. The posterior based on one measurement copied twice should therefore use one likelihood contribution, giving variance one half under this prior, rather than one third.","conclusion":"Fusion quality depends on dependence structure as much as on the number of input channels."}
limits: The Gaussian formulas require their likelihood, prior and independence assumptions. Perfect duplication is an extreme example; partially correlated inputs need covariance estimation and can be ill-conditioned. Neither a narrow posterior nor a numerical fusion score alone establishes model adequacy.

title: Transfer learning needs a support and invariance assumption
revised_question: Under what assumptions can a source-domain loss estimate target-domain performance?
status: Corrected formulation or classical result with an explicit worked example
summary: Under the stated assumptions, R_T(f)=E_S[w(X)ℓ(f(X),Y)]. A region with positive target probability but zero source probability cannot be handled by finite importance weights. Its labels can change target risk without changing any source observations. The revised question exposes the mathematical assumptions behind an asserted benefit from transferring a model.
definitions_json: ["Let P_S and P_T be source and target joint distributions of (X,Y), with bounded loss ℓ(f(X),Y).","Covariate shift means P_T(Y|X)=P_S(Y|X) on relevant support, while the marginal distribution of X may differ.","If P_T^X is absolutely continuous with respect to P_S^X, let w=dP_T^X/dP_S^X. In a finite space this is the ratio of target to source probabilities."]
theorem_name: Transfer learning needs a support and invariance assumption
theorem_statement: Under the stated assumptions, R_T(f)=E_S[w(X)ℓ(f(X),Y)]. A region with positive target probability but zero source probability cannot be handled by finite importance weights. Its labels can change target risk without changing any source observations.
theorem_proof: Condition on X. Shared conditionals make the conditional expected loss g(X)=E[ℓ(f(X),Y)|X] the same in both domains. Then R_T=∫g dP_T^X=∫wg dP_S^X=E_S[wℓ]. This uses the Radon–Nikodym change of measure, not a claim that any transferred representation preserves the conditional law. For the obstruction, place all source mass at X=0 and all target mass at X=1. Two data-generating worlds can agree on the source label Y=0 at zero but assign opposite labels at one. Every source dataset is identically distributed in both worlds, while a fixed predictor has different target error. Source-only risk estimation cannot distinguish them.

Weights are 1/3 at zero and three at one, so weighted source risk is (1/4)·3=3/4 exactly. The identity works because both target points occur in the source. It fails to supply an estimator in the support-gap example, where the required ratio at one has a zero denominator.","conclusion":"The revised question exposes the mathematical assumptions behind an asserted benefit from transferring a model."}

extension: For losses in [0,1] and weights bounded by M, a simple second-moment bound is E_S[(wℓ)²]≤M E_S[w]=M. It quantifies one reason that overlap and controlled density ratios matter for reliable transfer.

title: PCA reconstruction rank is not intrinsic dimension
revised_question: Which dimension is measured by a covariance spectrum, and what information is changed by a neighborhood embedding?

For the uniform unit circle,Σ=I/2; every rank-one projector leaves error1/2 despite the curve being one-dimensional. The revised question prevents a variance threshold or a visually compelling embedding from being reported as a theorem about intrinsic dimension.

It has one angular parameter and a two-dimensional affine span."]
theorem_name: PCA reconstruction rank is not intrinsic dimension
theorem_statement: If eigenvalues areλ₁≥⋯≥λ_d≥0, the optimal rank-k linear reconstruction error isΣ_{j>k}λ_j. For the uniform unit circle,Σ=I/2; every rank-one projector leaves error1/2 despite the curve being one-dimensional.

Moving weight from a smallerλ to a larger one cannot reduce this sum, so its maximum is the sum of the k largest eigenvalues. This proves the PCA claim directly. On the circle, angular averages of cos² and sin² are1/2 and the cross average is zero. Thus both eigenvalues are positive and equal, and every line loses exactly half the variance. theorem_proof: For the line, N_r=q^r; substitute into the exponential and use −log(1−u)=Σu^r/r. The projective line has one additional point, adding the factor 1/(1−t). Also Symⁿ(A¹) is affine n-space because an unordered multiset of n roots is encoded by the coefficients of its monic polynomial. This explains the symmetric-power coefficient qⁿ in that example. For the elliptic curve, count each right-hand-side value and its square roots, then add the point at infinity. The standard elliptic zeta theorem supplies the degree-two form; comparing the first coefficients gives N₁=q+1−a and N₂=q²+1−(a²−2q). The finite counts verify this instance but are not a proof of that theorem for every curve.

Exact finite-field enumeration over F₂₅ gives 26 affine points plus infinity. Since a²−2q=9−10=−1, the predicted extension count is 25+1−(−1)=27. The inverse local elliptic L-factor is 1/(1+3·5^(−s)+5·5^(−2s)); it is not the full point-counting zeta function with its extra degree-zero and degree-two factors. The recovered symmetric-power series has a precise point-counting interpretation: an effective zero-cycle is a nonnegative sum of closed points. A closed point of degree d contributes the geometric series(1−t^d)⁻¹. Multiplying over closed points gives the generating series of their multisets; taking its logarithm yieldsΣ_r N_r t^r/r, because a degree-d point contributes d rational points exactly over extension degrees divisible by d. This connects the symmetric-power generating function, Euler product and exponential point counts under the declared finite-field interpretation.","conclusion":"The arithmetic determinant must identify the object and degree it represents. Concrete point counts can check a proposed factor and expose a mismatched numerator or denominator."}

summary: The recovered assistant passage mentions CNOT entanglement and Lindblad decoherence. A Bell pair undergoing local dephasing yields an exact channel, a closed-form density matrix and a precise observability distinction between individual marginals and joint correlations.

theorem_proof: In the Z basis, ZρZ keeps diagonal entries and reverses off-diagonal signs. Thus the generator leaves diagonal entries fixed and gives derivative−γρ_01 for off-diagonal entries; the solution multiplies them by q. The displayed mixture has exactly that action. Its Kraus operators are K₀=√((1+q)/2)I and K₁=√((1−q)/2)Z. Both coefficients are nonnegative because0≤q≤1, and ΣK_j†K_j=I. A Kraus representation proves complete positivity, including after tensoring with an arbitrary ancilla, while the last identity proves trace preservation. For the Bell input, the only nonzero entries are the two populations1/2 and coherences q/2 linking00 and11. Partial traces remove those coherences, leaving I/2, whereas X⊗X exchanges00 and11 and therefore reads their sum q. Z⊗Z is+1 on both populated states.

status: Classical mathematics with newly authored derivation or finite example and explicit scope
summary: The historical gyre fragment adds undefined corrections to beta functions, vacuum energy, a magnetic moment and a holographic entropy. This exactly matches the four-parameter family of indistinguishable decompositions. If θ is fixed by an independent calibrated model, then g=F−θ is algebraically determined by the observation. title: An undefined Ψ measure needs an actual transport law

summary: The surviving label does not define a mathematical theory. A precise replacement is to ask what a measurable coordinate transport preserves. title: Ψ mutual information and capacity need a channel

summary: A channel capacity is an optimization over input distributions for a declared conditional law. It cannot be obtained by attaching a new symbol to mutual information. title: Functorial relabeling does not automatically preserve code distance
revised_question: Which structure does the proposed transformation preserve: composition, probability, metric distance, or computational difficulty?
status: Revised classical development with scoped worked result
summary: A genuine categorical transport can preserve every composition law while changing the usual Hamming distance of a code. This small counterexample separates structural equivalence from a coding guarantee. It also explains why naming a category cannot supply a cryptographic hardness assumption: additional metric or computational structure must be part of the objects and morphisms.
definitions_json: ["A binary length-n code is a subset C⊆{0,1}ⁿ. Its minimum distance is the least Hamming distance between distinct codewords. A category has identity maps and associative composition; a transport by bijections ψ_X sends f:X→Y to ψ_Y f ψ_X⁻¹."]

theorem_statement: The transported maps preserve identity and composition. An ambient Hamming isometry is sufficient to preserve every code’s pairwise distances and minimum distance; transporting the metric also preserves all distances. Preserving every ambient pairwise distance is exactly the isometry condition. A non-isometric map may nevertheless preserve a particular code or its minimum distance.

title: Euler’s product yields an exact partition recurrence

summary: A numerical deformation of Frobenius traces is not a rank theorem. For the same curve, a short exact argument proves a genuine rank lower bound by identifying a non-torsion rational point. This separates an established statement from the much stronger BSD claim.

Every nontrivial finite abelian group has an element of prime order, so rational torsion is trivial. The point(0,0) lies on the curve and differs from O; it is therefore non-torsion. A non-torsion element supplies a copy of Z inside E(Q), proving the rank lower bound. This does not require knowing the analytic order of vanishing of L(E,s). The two reduction primes are used asymmetrically only to respect the prime-to-p restriction. In general, gcd(#E(Fp),#E(Fq))=1 at distinct good primes does not justify simply quoting an unrestricted injection twice; the proof must separately exclude possible p-primary and q-primary torsion. title: A Benford law needs logarithmic equidistribution
revised_question: What theorem would justify a leading-digit law, and why does a coefficient deformation not supply it?

summary: The September 10 assistant claim gives no usable definition or asymptotic proof of a deformed Benford law for elliptic coefficients. A sound formulation reduces leading digits to fractional logarithms and proves an exact model where equidistribution is available.

theorem_name: A sufficient criterion and a proved model
theorem_statement: If the fractional parts of log10x_n are uniformly distributed on[0,1), then digit d has limiting frequency log10(1+1/d). For x_n=10^(nθ), every irrational θ satisfies this criterion.
theorem_proof: The digit event is precisely the interval in the definition, whose length is log10(d+1)−log10d. Uniform distribution gives its limiting frequency. For the model sequence and every nonzero integer k, the exponential average is N⁻¹Σ_(n=1)^N exp(2πiknθ). It is a geometric sum with ratio q=exp(2πikθ)≠1. Its magnitude is at most2/(N|1−q|), which tends to zero. Weyl’s criterion therefore yields uniform distribution. The nonvanishing denominator is where irrationality is used. In contrast, x_n=10^n always begins with1; rapid growth alone is insufficient. A nonlinear change of the index or coefficients needs a new equidistribution argument, because it changes the logarithmic sequence. The exponential-sum estimate depends onk through|1−exp(2πikθ)|. It proves convergence for every fixed nonzerok but does not give a uniform discrepancy bound over allk. A quantitative digit error estimate needs additional Diophantine control or an explicit finite-frequency approximation of the interval indicator.

Replacing n by n+1 in the normalization changes the limit by a factor tending to1, and the endpoints contribute vanishing weight. title: A Toeplitz log determinant needs positivity
revised_question: When is the logarithmic symbol integral a valid determinant limit, and what does it actually compute?
status: Classical result; recovered proposal repaired
summary: The historical use of an integral of log f resembles a Toeplitz determinant theorem, but it was inserted into an undefined decay model. A positive tridiagonal family gives an exact determinant recurrence and an independently derived limiting logarithm.
definitions_json: ["Let T_n=tridiag(b,a,b) with a>2|b| and D_n=detT_n; set D_0=1.","Define r_±=(a±√(a²−4b²))/2. For b≠0, 0<r_-<r_+; b=0 is immediate."]

theorem_statement: D_n=(r_+^(n+1)−r_-^(n+1))/(r_+−r_-), and lim n⁻¹logD_n=logr_+=π⁻¹∫₀πlog(a+2b cosθ)dθ.
theorem_proof: Expansion along the last row gives D_n=aD_(n−1)−b²D_(n−2), with D_0=1,D_1=a. Solving this second-order recurrence yields the formula, as its two characteristic roots are r_±. Factor r_+^(n+1) to obtain logD_n=(n+1)logr_++log[1−(r_-/r_+)^(n+1)]−log(r_+−r_-). Division by n gives the limit. Independently, the preceding eigenvalue formula and the positivity bound λ_k≥a−2|b|>0 permit the continuous test F=log, so the same limit is the symbol integral. This proves the integral identity without importing a decay interpretation. Positivity supplies a consistent real logarithm and bounds it on the entire spectral interval. Positive definiteness can also be verified without eigenvectors: the quadratic form is aΣu_j²+2bΣu_ju_(j+1), bounded below by(a−2|b|)Σu_j² using2|uv|≤u²+v². Thus every finite determinant is positive under the same hypothesis, independently confirming that its real logarithm is legitimate.

title: The atomic Hardy-space inequality requires cancellation
revised_question: What missing cancellation hypothesis makes the recovered local L²-to-H¹ estimate correct?
status: Classical result; recovered proposal repaired
summary: The recovered inequality is a standard atomic estimate once the function has mean zero. Omitting cancellation materially changes the theorem. The normalization can be proved in one line, but specifying the ambient real Hardy space and the atom conditions is essential.

The single-term representation g=λa gives the stated upper bound by the infimum definition. Also Cauchy–Schwarz gives ||a||₁≤1, so atomic convergence in coefficient sum entails L¹ convergence and preserves zero integral. Consequently every function represented by these global atoms has integral0. A nonnegative nonzero compactly supported bump has positive integral and cannot satisfy this global atomic H¹ condition, even though it has finite support and finite L² norm. title: A sublinear signed deformation is a homeomorphism, with a cusp at zero
revised_question: When does x↦x+α sign(x)|x|^β define a globally invertible coordinate change, and what regularity does it lose?
status: Classical result; recovered proposal repaired
summary: The historical radial correction becomes a precise real-variable map once its sign and parameter range are fixed. It is invertible for every α>0 and 0<β<1, but its derivative is unbounded near zero. This distinction matters whenever the map is inserted into a differential equation or metric.
definitions_json: ["Let φ(x)=x+α sign(x)|x|^β and φ(0)=0.","A map is inverse 1-Lipschitz when |φ⁻¹(u)−φ⁻¹(v)|≤|u−v| for all u,v."]
theorem_name: Global inversion and regularity
theorem_statement: For α>0 and 0<β<1, φ is an increasing homeomorphism R→R. Its inverse is 1-Lipschitz. The map φ is smooth off zero and fails to have a finite derivative at zero.
theorem_proof: The signed power s(x)=sign(x)|x|^β is continuous and strictly increasing. Thus for y>x, φ(y)−φ(x)=(y−x)+α[s(y)−s(x)]≥y−x>0. This proves injectivity and the inverse Lipschitz inequality. The limits at positive and negative infinity are respectively positive and negative infinity; continuity and the intermediate value theorem give surjectivity. A continuous strictly monotone bijection has a continuous inverse. For x≠0, φ′(x)=1+αβ|x|^(β−1)>1. At zero, φ(h)/h=1+α|h|^(β−1), which diverges as h→0. Consequently a smooth change-of-variables theorem requiring a finite nonzero derivative cannot be invoked at zero. There is a useful local Hölder estimate as well: for0<β<1, the signed power is β-Hölder with constant at most2^(1−β). On a bounded interval, φ therefore has a quantitative modulus of continuity even though it is not Lipschitz at zero. This separates continuity, differentiability and inverse stability.

title: An irrational angular frequency does not define a closed polar curve
revised_question: Under what hypotheses does an angular series descend from R to the circle and describe a closed planar curve?
status: Classical result; recovered proposal repaired
summary: The recovered “irrational monogon” series must first pass a periodicity test. A formula on the real angular line is not automatically a function on the quotient circle R/(2πZ). Without that descent, closing the curve and assigning its homology are extra operations.
definitions_json: ["A function r:R→R descends to S¹ precisely when r(θ+2π)=r(θ) for all θ.","For positive continuous periodic r, the map θ↦r(θ)(cosθ,sinθ) is a polar graph."]
theorem_name: A one-mode obstruction
theorem_statement: For a≠0 and ξ>0, r(θ)=1+a cos(ξθ) is 2π-periodic if and only if ξ is an integer. For irrational ξ, the endpoints of its restriction to [0,2π] have different radial distances.
theorem_proof: If r is periodic, evaluate at θ=0 to obtain cos(2πξ)=1, hence ξ is an integer. Conversely an integer frequency is periodic by the cosine addition formula. For irrational ξ, cos(2πξ)≠1, so r(2π)−r(0)=a[cos(2πξ)−1]≠0. The same polar direction at the two endpoints therefore has different radii. This proof does not automatically classify infinite sums: different frequencies can cancel, and their coefficients must be examined. It does show that irrationality by itself is not a mechanism producing a closed “one-sided” polygon. One may instead study an almost-periodic function on R, or add a closing segment, but those choices define different spaces. If a closing segment is explicitly added, the resulting loop can be studied, but its geometry depends on that segment. An endpoint identification in the parameter interval is a quotient construction instead and may fail to give a continuous planar map when the two endpoints have different images. These are distinct repairs.

Replacing √2 by3 makes the endpoint gap zero and produces a threefold periodic radial graph.","conclusion":"A continuous nonclosed arc and a simple closed curve have different topological models. The model must be chosen before computing homology."}

title: Regularity of the recovered lacunary angular series
revised_question: Which coefficient bounds make the angular series continuous or differentiable, before any geometric interpretation is attempted?
status: Classical result; recovered proposal repaired
summary: A meaningful infinite angular construction needs a convergence theorem. The same coefficients that control its size do not necessarily control its slopes: each differentiation multiplies the nth oscillation by ξ^n. This gives an explicit hierarchy of sufficient conditions.
definitions_json: ["Let ξ>1 and r(θ)=1+Σ_{n≥0}a_n cos(ξ^nθ).","For k≥0, put M_k=Σ_{n≥0}|a_n|ξ^(kn), allowing the value infinity."]
theorem_name: A sufficient regularity criterion
theorem_statement: If M_k is finite for an integer k≥0, the series defines a C^k function on R. Every derivative of order j≤k is obtained term by term and is uniformly bounded by M_j.
theorem_proof: The jth derivative of a_n cos(ξ^nθ) has absolute value at most |a_n|ξ^(jn). Since ξ>1 and j≤k, finiteness of M_k implies finiteness of M_j. The Weierstrass uniform convergence test therefore applies to every derivative series through order k. To justify differentiation, fix a base point and integrate the uniformly convergent first derivative series: the fundamental theorem of calculus identifies its integral with the uniform limit of the original partial sums.
